summary: Aparna Dhinakaran, co-founder of Arize AI, delivers a technical talk at the AI Engineer Summit 2025 on evaluating AI agents in production. She notes that while many talks cover building agents, this session focuses on ensuring they actually work reliably in the real world. Arize just announced its Series C round and is used by many teams to evaluate agents. She begins by highlighting the emerging frontier of voice AI, noting over 1 billion calls are made in call centers worldwide using voice assistants, and showcases Priceline's Pennybot as a real production multimodal agent that books vacations hands-free. She breaks down agents into three core components: the router (decides the next step, like a boss determining which skill to invoke), skills (logical chains that execute work, which may include LLM calls and API calls), and memory (stores multi-turn conversation state). She demonstrates these components using an open-source trace visualization of a code-based agent. For evaluation, she identifies three critical areas: router evaluation (did it call the right skill with correct parameters), skill-level evaluation (RAG chunk relevance, answer correctness, LLM-as-judge and code-based evals), and convergence (ensuring the agent takes a consistent, succinct number of steps). She notes different model providers can yield wildly different step counts. For voice applications, she explains that audio chunks need their own evals covering intent, speech quality, and speech-to-text accuracy, in addition to transcript text evaluation. She concludes by showing how Arize dogfoods its own co-pilot agent, running evals at every layer of the trace—overall response correctness, router selection, argument passing, and skill execution—emphasizing that evals must be distributed throughout the application so engineers can pinpoint whether failures occur at the router level, skill level, or elsewhere in the flow.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Context
sections.summary: Aparna introduces herself as co-founder of Arize AI, mentions their Series C announcement, and frames the talk as focusing on evaluating agents in production rather than just building them.

sections.title: Voice AI and Multimodal Agents
sections.summary: Discusses voice AI taking over call centers with over 1 billion calls worldwide, showcases Priceline's Pennybot as a production multimodal agent, and notes that voice/multimodal agents require specialized evaluation beyond text-only agents.

sections.title: Components of an Agent: Router, Skills, Memory
sections.summary: Defines the three core components: router (decides next step, like a boss), skills (logical chains doing the work, including LLM and API calls), and memory (stores multi-turn conversation state). Notes these patterns are common across frameworks like LangGraph, CrewAI, and LlamaIndex.

sections.title: Demo: Code-Based Agent Trace
sections.summary: Demonstrates an open-source trace visualization showing a code-based agent answering a query about trace latency, with multiple router calls, a SQL query tool call, and a data analyzer skill, illustrating how router, skills, and memory interact.

sections.title: Evaluating Agents: Router, Skills, and Convergence
sections.summary: Covers three evaluation areas: router (correct skill with correct parameters), skills (RAG relevance, answer correctness, LLM-as-judge and code-based evals), and convergence (consistent step counts, noting different model providers yield wildly different paths). Audience interaction confirms few teams currently evaluate router-level or convergence.

sections.title: Voice Application Evaluation
sections.summary: References movie 'Her' to illustrate the complexity of voice applications. Explains that voice agents require evaluating audio chunks, user sentiment, speech-to-text transcription accuracy, and tone consistency, in addition to transcript text evaluation.

sections.title: Dogfooding Arize's Co-pilot and Multi-Layer Evals
sections.summary: Shows how Arize evaluates its own co-pilot agent, running evals at every layer of the trace: overall response correctness, router selection, argument passing, and skill execution. Emphasizes that evals must be distributed throughout the application so engineers can pinpoint whether failures occur at the router level, skill level, or elsewhere. Concludes the talk and takes audience questions.
